title: Our Embodied Life, Part 3: Who is Senjo?
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: The talk explores how our experiences shape us into who we are, and how we can come to understand our true essence beyond these roles and personas. It's not about losing ourselves, but recognizing and inhabiting our fundamental nature, which is often hidden beneath layers of conditioning and circumstance. By letting go of attachments and acknowledging the influence of external causes, we can discover a deeper sense of self that is more authentic and whole.

sentences.text: Good evening, everyone.
It's great to see everyone on yet another beautiful summer evening.
This is the third in our series about the embodied life.
It's an apt title for the series, particularly tonight, because we're talking about which body it is, which manifestation of our life we're living, and how we understand that.
As you sit and listen tonight, and you listen out of your zazen, remember again that this story is your story.
I'll be telling the story of a Chinese folk tale, and a boy and a girl, a man and a woman who lived back then.
Listen for the reverberations of your own life and your own experiences.
I'll speak more out of mine because that's what I know.
But as you're allowing it in, imagine the storyline being your storyline.
The way this koan is normally referred to is Senjo and her soul are separated.
It's case 35 of the Mumonkan, which we've been studying off and on over the last few months.
It's one of the two, I think, that are actually folk tales.
So they're not pithy exchanges primarily between a student and a teacher, but a story that a teacher has found deeply meaningful.
I will talk about it first from the point of view of the narrative, from the usual storyline and how we think about our lives as that usual storyline.
Then we'll speak about it from a Zen question.
But even as we speak about it as our narrative, hold open the question of who is the real Senjo.
Who is the true Senjo?
That's the question that Goso, Master Wutsu, asks his students about this well-known folk tale.
Tonight I'm going to tell the story instead of us all reading it, so that you can settle into your own story as you hear my voice.
Somewhere far away, long ago, in Kaohsiung, China, there was a father, Shokan, and his beautiful daughter Senjo, who was the second of his two daughters.
The first had died young, leaving the family just one precious child.

You'll hear different versions, you'll read different versions, so I'm going to include different ways it's been presented so you can hear different perspectives, just like you might hear different perspectives in your own life.
So here's this beautiful little girl, and Shokan has a nephew named Ochu.
Senjo and Ochu play a lot together as children, and they get along so well that the father jokes, "Someday I'll marry the two of you, you'll be betrothed."
They either believe it and feel like a promise is made, this is ancient China, or they come to feel more and more fond of each other.
Maybe they're even encouraged to feel more and more fond of each other.
So they grow up that way.
Then at some point, as Senjo gets to be older, she has many suitors because she's very beautiful, this precious girl.
The father decides it's time to make an actual choice of a husband, and he's going to marry her well, to a young man who's very promising, named Hinryu.
Well, you can imagine when Ochu and Senjo hear this, they're both really startled and upset, aggrieved, grieving.
Depending on the story you read, Ochu either can't bear the pain of thinking that the young woman he loves is going to be married to someone else, or he's infuriated, and he decides he has to leave.
Without telling anyone, he loads up a little canoe, a little boat, and late at night he sets sail down the river.
Somewhere along the river path, maybe it's around midnight, he sees a figure running.
He might recognize her immediately as Senjo, or he might see the shadowy figure and wonder who it is, and stop.
He thinks he hears his name.
And lo and behold, who is it but his beloved, Senjo.
He's overwhelmed with relief and delight to see her again, so joyous, and of course she joins him in the boat.
They continue on, go many cities or towns along the river, and settle themselves someplace that's reasonably far away.
They're together for five or six years, and have two beautiful children.
All the while, there's a certain degree of disquietude within Senjo.
Her father had made a promise to someone else, and it was her role to fulfill it, and she wanted to go home.
She missed her parents, and she's raising her two beautiful children away from her grandparents.
She wanted to go home and bring her children there, maybe to make apologies, maybe to see how they actually were.
Without her knowing, Ochi was actually thinking the same thing.
He really wanted to go too.
He missed his family.
So they prepare the boat and sail upriver, and when they land in the village, Ochi says, "No, no, you wait here, let me go and apologize, let me go and see how it really is there."
So he goes up to Chokan's home, ready to make obeisance and make his apologies, and he starts out to say something.
The father interrupts him, saying, "Oh, I'm so happy to see you, I've been so worried about you.
You disappeared, and we didn't know what happened to you.
I'm so glad to know that you're all right."
At which point Ochi is choked up, because he knows that he's done something very hurtful.
He continues to make his apologies and says, "I'm so sorry, you know that your daughter and I ran away together.
We have a family, we're here to apologize and be reunited with you."
Chokan gets very quiet, and he looks confused, and he says, "What do you mean?
No, no, when you left, Senjo took to the bed.
She hasn't spoken.
She hasn't spoken for five years since you left."
At which point Ochi is thinking, "Oh my god, what's going on here?"
Is he being manipulative?
He starts to get a little short-fused, I guess maybe.
And he says, "No, no, no, you don't understand.
She's with me.
She's with me.
Come down to the boat with me."
So the father sends the servant down with Ochi, and there in fact he sees Senjo, and comes back and says, "She's there."
In the meantime, Ocho goes into the house and sees a pale, ghost-like figure lying in the bed that looks exactly like Senjo.
When her father tells her the story, that actually Senjo's there, she gets this look of relief, delight on her face.
She gets up and walks out of the house at the same time that the woman with the two children, Senjo, walks up, and they smile at each other and somehow become one.
And Senjo, who was the daughter in the bed, that voice speaks and says, "All this time gone by, I didn't know whether I left in a dream or if it was really me."
So the question is, what happened?
Who is who?
What was what?
Whose imagination?
In a certain kind of way, we live like that too, trying to figure out who we really are.
As I study this, I realize this koan is a bit of the Genjokoan.
Is it not?
To study the self is our first imperative, one of the most important things Dogen says to us.
So who is the self?
I think a lot of the early part of our lives, maybe the first 30, 40, 70 years, is about trying to figure out who we really are.
The story works in one way.
It works in those kinds of motifs.
There are family expectations.
Senjo has expectations and hopes.
So does Ocho.
They each have a narrative of their life that's put into motion very early on, like we do.
They have their own emotionality, their own love, desire, attachment, the human and animal elements that we all are and we manifest in different ways.
There are the psychological elements of what's happening, and the family dynamics and the traditions, the cultural and historical roles, and our developmental roles.
They're young.
There's a time to rebel.
There's a time to do something other than what you think you should do, to define who you are, to really come to understand it.
Of course, we have all of those experiences too.
You take a moment and you review your life, whether it's 80 years or whether it's 25 years, you'll really reflect on those kinds of experiences.
We have our family roles, our developmental stages of exploration and individuation, and our culture.
Autonomy matters a great deal in figuring out who we are in that way, defining our gender and how to express it.
We have bodies.
We're being bodies.
We come to inhabit our bodies with all of what that means.
It means exploring man or woman, transgender.
It's exploring size and aptitude.
It's exploring race, our own reactions to it, how we internalize, and how we're oblivious, depending upon what our situation is.
We realize that we walk around in a particular body in this world, and that influences very much who we are and how we see things.
But we don't often inhabit that entirely.
We kind of take it for granted, this thing that we walk around.
So we have our ideas of ourselves, and I think we also realize who we are in relationship to others.
It's very profound, actually, recognizing the mirrors in other people's reactions, expressions, the friendships we develop.

We come to understand in our family if we're going to be the caretaker, the one to succeed, to live the family legacy, to be the good businessman or the professional, the troublemaker or the wanderer.
We may have some idealized idea of who we are, as a hero, our own hero or heroine.
If our parents were Roosevelt Democrats, maybe we're meant to do good.
If your parents were back-to-the-landers when you grew up, maybe it means you want a suit and a tie for security.
Our personal manifestation in our life takes shape around many roles over time, and roles specific to a given time or place.
Today, you may have functioned as a father, a husband, a boss, a student, a teacher, a consumer.
I don't know what all.
We are much like Sencha.
We change between these roles at any given time or hour.
Over time, we look back with amazement over all the different people we've been.
If you've lived any period of time, don't you sometimes look back and you go, "Oh, I was a bodybuilder.
Oh, I hitchhiked across Central America.
Who is that?"
And on and on.
One of my dear Dharma brothers in Berkeley, when he retired, he was a very beloved elementary teacher for many years.
He gave a student talk in which he said, "Now that I'm retired, I'm going to look back to those things that really gave me pleasure when I was 10.
And I'm going to pick those back up again, because that tells me something about who I really am."
We come into our different expressions in life, and do we lose track of something?
Where is it?
Really?
Are we really one or the other of any of these roles at any time?
Are we two or one?
The Genjokoan says to study the self is to forget the self, right?
So what does that mean?
It's easy to get tripped up on this and say, "Yeah, well, do everything and nothing, right?"
It's really not that easy.
It's a facile answer.
Goso gave this as a koan.
It was considered one of the Nanto koans, which means one of the ones that helps point at the separate within the absolute.
It's easy to fall into the idea that emptiness is it.
You know, you're not attached to anything, anything goes, everything's all right.
But is it really just one?
When you forget the self, what is that self?
We fall into the absolute and we think that we're all of it.
But actually in any moment we're being thoroughly what is being called for.
What's being called for calls up all of ourself.
It's what Dogen calls practice realization.
Actualizing the fundamental point of our lives is to express everything here and now.
There are shadow sides to this idea of falling into the absolute.

It's easy to identify too strongly with the role, to see ourselves as the role, the doctor, the teacher, the therapist, who, the police officer, who maybe takes on so much of that persona that they are not at all in touch with the rest of who they are or how they are.
It's also quite possible, living in this absolute, to deny that we are in that role.
We're everything and anything, right?
"For many years I'm not really a doctor.
I just do this thing.
I just do this."
Well, who am I?
Kidding.
I'm totally defined in that moment, in that role with that other person in the room, by their hopes, expectations, ideas, and my need to respond to it.
That's one complete definition.
How do I inhabit that?
We can't escape our roles because they're co-created.
Senjo was not a daughter without a father.
A doctor cannot be a doctor without a patient.
A white person cannot be a white person to a black person and vice versa.

Our responsibility is to inhabit all of who we are, all of the roles of our realities, and to investigate and understand them, to understand how we relate to them, and to try and see how we're related to.
It's like taking the jewel of our lives in our hands and turning over the many facets, feeling it, inhabiting it, coming to know it.
The way my teacher talks about this, I think, is in essence and function.
Our function at any given moment might be being dad, but it's not just with your dad hat on.
You're actually bringing all of your life to that moment.
Our essence is not just some absolute enlightened form.

Our essence is like the Sambhogakaya, that body of Buddha that is pure activity, that manifests wisdom, that manifests compassion, that is the activity of the Buddha Dharma in that moment expressed through the individuality of your life, all of your life.
Whether we know it or not, all of our life is playing out in who and how we are.
We may think that we're just being mother, or we're just being teacher, or just being whatever, but it's not so.
Everyone is there.
Mostly we have a sense of times operating behind the veil of some ideas of ourselves, but that essence is when we're really completely in touch with it.
That veil is kind of like a clothing style, an affect, or a midlife crisis that's about something else.
The essence is always there.
Sometimes we say that Zen practice is to live an authentic life.
That's not quite right.
You can quibble with that.
I think what we do is authentic, but it's to inhabit our life completely.
It's to fill out all of these different experiences, ways of being in the world, and roles.
The title of this koan is often, most often, Senjo and her soul are separated.
I thought about that, and none of the commentaries I could find actually commented on that.
But actually, what's the Buddhist idea of a soul anyway?
In fact, that was one of the ideas of Indian philosophy that Buddha strongly would not comment on.
A soul becomes a something.
I think really it's the essence.
The essence and the function, perhaps, were not unified, as they so often are not unified in our lives.
We're functioning, but we're not as often completely connected.
I think of this as fundamentalness, our most fundamental nature.
When you're quiet, to me, it seems like it's a feeling, the voice of your inmost request, that which really informs your life, which gives your life its light, its expression.
It's expressed out of our vows, too.
We take these vows as an expression of the fundamentalness of our life.
Then we play it out in many different ways throughout a lifetime.
One of the key points in the story is that when the Senjos meet, they smile at each other.
It's a smile of recognition.

I think, for me, one of those moments was when I saw my birth mother's picture, and I saw myself completely, and I understood something about what this person's essence was that I had never understood before.
I thought it was something I could erase or transform through therapy.
It was such a relief to know I was just stuck with me.
It might be when you see your true vocation, that moment.
It might be when you meet someone who will be your friend for 50 years, and you just know it, or you meet your future partner.
That moment of recognition of something whole within yourself: the Senjos meet and smile.
It's the same experience in the transmission story, the first transmission of the Dharma story between Shakyamuni and Makhapashapa, where Shakyamuni holds up a flower and turns it.
Most of you know that story, and Makhapashapa smiles.
He recognizes the true nature of things, his true nature.

When we wholeheartedly engage with all the parts of ourselves and their expression in the present circumstances, we are completely ourselves, giving life to our role in any moment, studying our lives, who it is who is here.
To forget the self is to forget ideas of who we are and to actually be who we are, our spontaneous, original selves.
Can I wholeheartedly be here?
Can I see the ways in which I check out, deny the role, become the role, resist the role, to study this?
Senjo denies one role and becomes another, but who is she really?
Goso's verse from the Mumonkan, his commentary on it, is this.
*Clouds and mountain, sorry, clouds and the moon are the same.
Valleys and mountains are different.
All are blessed.
All are blessed.
Not two, not one.*
Clouds and the mountain.
Clouds are everyday, ever-changing selves, and the moon, our idea of the absolute or enlightenment.
Valleys and mountains are daily ups and downs, experiences, living and being.
All are blessed.
All are blessed.
One is not higher than the other.
One is not something to attain, to leave the other behind.
Not two, not one.
What's your expression?
This separation that we try to unify with time, at times, sometimes more successfully, perhaps with more study, a little more completely.
That separation is the fulcrum of being human.
It's the blessing of being human, that our lives are divided and we're asked over and over again to study the truth of this separation and this wholeness, to understand.
And I think you understand it more and more deeply the longer you practice, a certain kind of loneliness that comes from knowing that the separation is real.
Senjo dreams after the reunion, or maybe she says after the reunion, *I dreamed I ran after the boat, but I couldn't tell who it was that ran away.* Was it me?
Was it not me?
Not knowing opens to a greater intimacy.
Is it one or is it two who ran over after the boat?
So I'll stop there and that gives us time.

Perhaps it's an opportunity for anyone who wants to speak for yourself of your experience of coming to understand your essence, your function, the way in which your life expresses itself through the various ways you have to interact with the world, or you've come to understand it through the ways the world is mirrored to you.
And although we won't go around or call on people, I'd really like to invite everyone to consider offering something.
We have about 20, 25 minutes to do that.
Oh, thank you.
I hope this isn't a downer.
I'm in a confusion and transition because I am now actually old and feeling it and slowing down.
And as many of you know, I was ordained as a priest three years ago and am expecting to go forward serving robustly this sangha.
And I do some things, but I can't do what I used to do.
So I don't know what my role is.
It's undefined.
Cramped up about that.
Definitely it isn't one, or it isn't the same one.
I don't know what it is.
And I'm surprised that this has happened.
But I see my peer group, the same thing.
This year everything stopped.
More rest needed.
More gazing into space.
It's pretty interesting.
I'm healthy, I'm glad to say.
But I'm in a weird warp right now.
So I hope you'll tolerate me while I come through the tunnel of some kind.
And I just want you to know that actually things do change when you get old.
It doesn't just look like it, it actually is.
Thank you.
I'll start by saying I really appreciate the talk.
The story and the entire talk in general has really hit home.
I thought it was really interesting when you brought up your friend who said you're gonna go back to doing what they did when they were 10 years old.

Because when you were telling that story, and the soul lying in the bed, that's what I often think about in my own life: what sort of things from when you were younger have you forgotten about now that you're starting your career path and are in school and have actual responsibility in life?

There's definitely some things that have fallen to the wayside, and it's almost like you just don't enjoy them as much anymore because you don't have as much time to really devote to those things that you used to, so carefree.
I don't know too much what else to say about it, but I think it's very good to look back to when we were a little younger, when we were kids, and what we enjoyed doing.
Where are those interests and energy now?
Where are those interests and what was in them for you now?
As far as what sort of enjoyment did I get from them and where did that enjoyment go?
One of them I can bring up is drawing.
I used to really enjoy just pencil and paper, and I could sit there for hours and hours and hours and draw.
Well, now I'm in school and work, and I think to myself, I have time to sit down and draw.
I might be drawing, but I'm not there in the moment drawing, just having a good time.
I'm thinking about work and thinking about my next meal and thinking about what do I have to do next and where's the money going to come from for this and what's going to happen with school.
It's been to at least not forget about those things.
Keep with an attachment.
Not just what the interest was but the creativity, the attention to detail, the use of your body.

I've struck a little bit about over my life I've worn many different uniforms, and in many ways it's like putting a uniform on, in the sense that I don't think we have this perception that we are pretty constant, but it's not true.

Me at work, as another physician, I am the doctor, and you sort of flow into that persona and that's who you are for whatever eight or twelve hours, and then you go home and you're not that person anymore.
You're somebody different.
The expectations are different.
You're different, and some of your core values may be mostly similar.
I don't even know that they're all the same.
It's interesting how much we change in the various roles that we assume in our life.
Being a parent, a child, even as a grown man.
I'm in my 50s but I'm still the child of my mother, who is now my child because she's losing her memory, and so there's now assuming a role of parent with my mother.
It's just interesting how much things change.
We think we're the same person.
There's a way in which we change psychologically.
We change in our maturity and our stability and handling things.
We change, I think, in our wisdom just after having lived periods of time.
As well as we change our function and relationship.

One of the, without wanting to take too much of the conversation, one of the really interesting questions, so I do geriatrics for those of you who don't know that, and so I take care of a lot of people who are on that slope of their lives where they're changing a lot.
You don't notice you change so much during your 20s, 30s, and 40s, and then it begins to pick up a little bit of momentum.
You reach a point where it's really perceptible over a period of months and sometimes faster than that.
There's often a deep dissociation between who I am and what's actually happening.
I really see my work as helping people find their wholeness, because the person that you've always been is still there.
That essence of what informs your life and what informs your person is still there, even though you're not doing the same things you were.
You can't perform your roles in the same way.
You've become a child instead of a parent, but it's really profound that people still are themselves in some really fundamental way.
Please.
I really enjoyed the talk and so many things came up for me.
One is, if one was actually successful in forgetting the self, who is it who does the forgetting?
The other thing that struck me was Dongshan's Five Franks.
This old woman who looks back from the mirror, who is it?
The reflection is an old person, while the person looking into the mirror does not think old or young.
It thinks I, I, I, me, me, me, and this old person looks back.
And the third one is this idea, and I'm going to speak in I because I cannot speak for anybody else, this idea of who I am, what my core character is.
I always thought of myself, I am like this.
This is me.
This defines me.
Until in one lightning strike moment I had to recognize that this I that I so appreciated, that I was so proud of, was the result of stuff that happened to me as a child.
This fierce independence that I thought, I'm just this inherently independent person.
That was a reaction, a push, because certain things happened to me.
And to recognize, in this one moment, that this cherished I that I liked so much, that I polished, made it look really good, do you like it?
It was not the I.
It was conditioning, it was co-arising of two events.
So all these things came up for me during the talk, and probably another half dozen, but these are the ones that stuck around.
Thank you very much.
Please.
So I'm a nurse at a long-term care facility, so I understand exactly what you see, but I'm gonna reflect on it differently.
Those who are healthcare professionals know about long amounts of days in a row where you just keep working and working.
I just recently finished three weeks in a row of non-stop working, doing 12-hour shifts, and so for the last three weeks I've been driving towards the end.
It's very tiresome.
You doctors should understand that.
It gets really tiresome and you've got to be compassionate.
These people are, as you said, going through some changes, and you've got to be compassionate.
And that just clicked with me.
When I was trying to get through this, trying to be compassionate to people, I found myself walking into a room and just stopping myself first thing and going, I'm a nurse.
This is my job.
But now that I think about it, now that I hear it, for those last three weeks, even when I got home I was still like, I'm a nurse.
Sleep.
Get up.
I'm a nurse.
Get up.
Go to work.
Come back.
Go home.
Shower.
I'm a nurse.
I was just, because I had to, and also I just couldn't get through it.
I'm just so exhausted.
I haven't even gotten to sleep yet.
Because there were nights, I just couldn't sleep today.
But it became so focused on that role.
It was like I didn't have any role outside of that.
It's almost like returning home and wondering, okay, well now I'm not a nurse, and there's something there.
Then I kept having to remind myself, remind myself, these people are sick, and I'm getting really frustrated because everybody knows.
So I kept digging myself deeper and deeper and deeper into that role.
That one role.
And I had to.
I felt like I had to.
Right.
That balance between knowing I have to go to work, it's my job to go to work, and I have to do it in a way I'm going to feel good about.
So I'm a nurse.
Gosh, I have a body and I'm exhausted.
I just need to sit down.
I need to use the bathroom because I need to eat.
You have to integrate all of that and tune in.
It's difficult.
You know that you need to say I have to take a day off or I have to go take a break now.
But that's okay too.
I really appreciate what you're saying and I admire it.
I have some idea of how difficult that is.
Oh yes, Bob.
So this goes back maybe 30 years, many previous roles in my life, but working down at the legislature, I ended up in a role where I had to do some lobbying.

I went up and got my first three-piece new suit, and a friend and I went down to the office with the Ways and Means Committee chair and his assistant, and she said, just remember, as long as you can think of it as dressing up, you'll be okay.
It's always been a very helpful recognition.
Please, Marilyn.
I really appreciate the readings.
I've read them all a couple times, the handout and the book, and it went deeper each time.
I want to continue working with it.
One of the first things that comes to my mind when I think of who I am is that it's in the moment.
I always think of it as pure potential.
And what is the truth right now in this moment?
Can I feel the truth?
Do I know the truth?
It seems as I age it's easier.
I can feel when I'm out of sync, if I go to say something or do something or write something.
Is that real?
What is here right now in this moment?
I have a story a little bit like Eith's.
When I was a kid, mostly probably around 10 and 11, and what you're talking about, I used to ride horses a lot, and I was an inner-city kid and it took a lot to be able to do that.
But it was the thing in my life that really held my life together, because there was abuse, and I got so much out of that relationship with horses and the people that were there.
So about a year ago I started volunteering out at Animals as Natural Therapy and I just loved it.
I just fell in love with it.
I was with therapists and I was a mentor and I was with horses, and everything that I ever really cherished came back for me.
And I worked really well for about six months or so, maybe a little bit longer.
And then some fears came up.
I have very severe osteoporosis, and I tried to, I think I was really pretending a little bit there, hiding it a little bit.
But horses are 1200 pounds and they move quickly, and I don't have the same reactions as I used to.
And I just started realizing that, and I saw everyone that I was working with, and they were in their 30s and 20s mostly, except for a couple of therapists.
And I realized that I was uncomfortable a lot, as much as I was absolutely loving it and feeling this is my home.
It felt very much to me like sangha, just the personalities of the people and the attitude towards the kids that were coming and that we were working with.
And so it was a lot to give up.
And so it was a chance to touch my wellness again and a chance to realize what's real right now, and maybe this isn't the best thing for me, or I'm endangering other people to work with you.
So I gave that up a month or two ago.
But yeah, I think just this, one other quick story that fits with this: we learn to look deeply and to look deeper at who is this, what is this.

But I remember when we were ordained, the night before we were ordained, we met with one of the nuns that is one of Thich Nhat Hanh's highest teachers, and she gave us a sort of orientation before the ordination.

She said, when you make a mistake or when you do something that you regret, you need to be light about it, because there are so many causes and conditions in your life that you can never figure it out.

You talk about what affects you as a child and who made this personality, but there are so many things so much further back and so much deeper, things that you don't even know that influence you in that second, that moment when something happens.
And sometimes we just have to let it go and not take all that on and figure out who was that that did that.
We're just about out of time, but I wonder if there's anyone who, yeah, Terry.
What astounds me is sitting here realizing that there are all these causes and conditions that go way beyond my individual life, way beyond.
Who knows the origin of all this?
It's a complete mystery.
And I sit here now and I listen to everybody and it's astounding to me that right now, I do not say it, I am all that I'm hearing.
It's like the wind or the birds or something.
I am all that I'm hearing, and yet I am Terry, and what is that?
So I'm just really appreciating sitting here.

verbatim.text: Good evening, everyone. It's great to see everyone on yet another beautiful summer evening. So this is the third in our series about the embodied life.
